newsitem.title: USA: Colonial Pipeline prorates distillate line orders.
newsitem.headline: Colonial Pipeline prorates distillate line orders.

text.p: Colonial Pipeline Co, noting increased shipping orders since U.S. Department of Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary met with oil industry executives Friday, said it will allocate orders from Wednesday until the end of November.
A Colonial official also said Colonial will accept no more orders on the current 29th shipping cycle, which ends late Tuesday, and will open its 1.2 million bpd gasoline line to distillate shipments.

Colonial spokesman Noel Griese said Colonial opened its adjacent gasoline line to distillate shipments for at least the next 40 days through the 33rd cycle, which includes the last 10 days of November.
He said distillate allocations through the end of November were necessary because of a surge in shipping orders since Friday's meeting between O'Leary and heads of over a dozen oil companies.
Traders said cash heating oil and low sulphur diesel prices in Houston weakened about 0.75 cent a gallon after Colonial advised clients Monday afternoon of the allocations.
"It's a case of extremely low inventories and people want to ship as much as possible to the Northeast," one Gulf Coast trader said.
He pegged prompt USG heating oil at 3.50 cents below NYMEX heating oil for November delivery.
Griese noted Colonial president Donald Brinkley also attended the highly-publicized Washington, D.C. summit.

Griese noted that the Colonial distillate line, which normally can carry up to 960,000 barrels per day, is currently operating at only 720,000 barrels per day following repairs to a segment that ruptured in South Carolina last June.

With repairs now completed, he said Colonial is optimistic that "by early November" the federal Office of Pipeline Safety will lift restrictions that now limit pumping pressure in the affected area 100 miles northeast of Atlanta, Georgia.
The approval would allow Colonial to return the distillate line to full capacity, he said, although heavy demand would still require the pipeline to allocate space.
"Each shipper may call our computer to see how much they can nominate based on past volumes they have transported," he said.
